items.title: Female Reproductive Cycle - The Menstrual Cycle

source_refs.note: Topic 17.1.3 with the For Information boxes on menopause and hCG (PDF 79-82); Figures 17.6 and 17.7 are replaced by the original diagram. The chapter's exercises (PDF 81-82) are not part of the lesson body.

blocks.text: The female reproductive system works through a series of cyclic events, the menstrual cycle, which lasts about a month (28 days on average) and has three phases.

items: Menstrual phase (days 1 to 5): the functional layer of the endometrium is shed, and the tissue and blood leave the body (menstruation) for 3 to 5 days, because estrogen and progesterone are low. FSH begins to rise.

Proliferative phase and ovulation (days 6 to 14): the rise in FSH makes a few follicles grow, but only one, the Graafian follicle, matures and rises to the ovary's surface while the others degenerate. FSH makes it secrete estrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium, making it velvety, thick and supplied with blood. At the end of this phase (day 14) a sudden release of LH from the anterior pituitary makes the Graafian follicle release the ovum into the oviduct: ovulation.

Secretory (post-ovulatory) phase (days 15 to 28): LH turns the ruptured follicle into a yellow corpus luteum, which secretes estrogen and progesterone that make the endometrium more vascular and glandular. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, LH secretion stops, estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly and the thickened endometrium is shed with bleeding: menstruation on day 28.

blocks.alt: A chart over days 1 to 28. Top: follicles grow into a Graafian follicle, ovulation at day 14, then a corpus luteum that grows and breaks down. Middle: FSH fairly low with small rises, a sharp LH surge just before day 14, estrogen peaking before ovulation and again later, and progesterone high in the second half. Bottom: the uterine lining, shed in days 1 to 5, thickening to day 14 and thickest in the secretory phase.
blocks.caption: Changes in the ovary, hormones and uterus during the menstrual cycle (original diagram after Figures 17.6 and 17.7).
blocks.long_description: Menstrual phase (days 1 to 5): low estrogen and progesterone make the functional layer of the endometrium shed with blood; FSH begins to rise. Proliferative phase and ovulation (days 6 to 14): FSH makes a few follicles grow, one becoming the Graafian follicle, whose estrogen rebuilds the endometrium; around day 14 a sudden release of LH makes the Graafian follicle release the egg. Secretory phase (days 15 to 28): LH turns the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum, whose estrogen and progesterone make the endometrium more vascular and glandular; without fertilization the corpus luteum breaks down, the hormones fall and menstruation begins again.

blocks.title: Pregnancy and menopause
blocks.text: If the egg is fertilized, the tiny embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which keeps the corpus luteum alive, so estrogen and progesterone stay high and menstruation is prevented; because hCG comes from the embryo's chorion and not the mother, it is the hormone that pregnancy tests detect. The cycles stop at around 50 years of age: menopause.

blocks.title: Note on the text
blocks.text: The book says LH is released because FSH falls as estrogen rises. In most accounts it is the high, sustained level of estrogen just before ovulation that triggers the LH surge (positive feedback on the pituitary), with a smaller FSH peak at the same time. The figure shows this standard pattern.

blocks.prompt: What is the role of the corpus luteum, and what keeps it alive in pregnancy?
blocks.explanation: It secretes estrogen and progesterone that keep the endometrium thick, vascular and glandular. In pregnancy hCG from the embryo maintains it, so the lining is not shed.

items: Days 1-5 menstruation (low estrogen, progesterone); 6-14 FSH, Graafian follicle, estrogen, LH surge and ovulation; 15-28 corpus luteum, progesterone; no fertilization: hormones fall, cycle restarts.
hCG from the embryo keeps the corpus luteum; menopause at about 50.
